Q: Dynamics 365: why an assemby was found for real-time workflow but wosn't for the same background workflow? A:

One thing to verify is how the custom workflow activity is registered.

A custom workflow activity can be available only for specific execution modes depending on its registration metadata and the assembly version deployed to the server.

Things I would check are:

  1. Verify that the assembly is registered correctly and that the workflow activity appears in the Plug-in Registration Tool.

  2. Make sure the server where the Asynchronous Processing Service is running has the same assembly version as the one used by the web application. If the async service is running on a different server, an outdated assembly can cause activities to appear only in one workflow designer.

  3. Restart the Microsoft Dynamics 365 Asynchronous Processing Service after deploying a new version of the assembly, as it may continue using cached metadata.

  4. Confirm that the activity is not throwing a load exception. Fusion logs or the Windows Event Viewer may reveal assembly binding issues that do not appear in the workflow designer.

If the activity consistently appears in real-time workflows but never in background workflows after these checks, it would suggest that the asynchronous service cannot load the assembly rather than a problem with the workflow designer itself.

Q: OLE DB Provider for ODBC Drivers Error "80004005' A:

The simple solution in my scenario was also about supplying missing proper connection strings, so the given answers were helpful in pointing towards the specific root cause, i.e. an absent Global.asa¹ file, which provides connection strings at application scope, but wasn’t source-controlled, so it didn’t came along by itself when cloning the Classic ASP application.

(Noted to further exhaustiveness, because Application Pools, permissions, string format and method calling were all faultless.)

Q: This request contains scopes that cannot be requested together (youtube and drive.file) A:

solution is to use incremental authorization or separate OAuth flows.

Instead of requesting everything at once:

YouTube scopes + drive.file

do something like:

Flow 1 (YouTube):

youtube
youtube.upload
youtube.force-ssl
youtubepartner

After the user authorizes, if Drive access is needed:

Flow 2 (Drive):

drive.file

Google supports incremental authorization, so users don't need to re-approve previously granted scopes.

Check if youtubepartner is actually needed

Many applications don't need:

https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtubepartner

It is intended for YouTube CMS/content partners and is one of the most sensitive YouTube scopes.

If your app only uploads videos and manages the authenticated user's channel, you may only need:

youtube.upload
youtube
youtube.force-ssl

or even fewer, depending on the API calls you make.

Also verify

  • You're using the same OAuth client ID as before.

  • Both the YouTube Data API v3 and Google Drive API are enabled.

  • The OAuth consent screen hasn't been modified recently.

  • No recent changes were made to your Google Cloud project.

If nothing changed on your side

If your application worked for a year and stopped yesterday without any code changes, this strongly suggests a server-side policy change by Google rather than an issue in your application.

Q: How to automatically update the status of an enrollment in an ASP.NET Core Web API following Clean Architecture? A:

There are a lot of scenarios where you really don't need to update statuses in real time. If all reads use the same API, then the API can update EnrollmentStatus if and when the record is read.

In fact, if the only statuses are Active, Overdue, and Canceled and there aren't other complications that you didn't mention, then you don't even need EnrollmentStatus. You only need a Canceled property. When Canceled is false, you can calculate Active or Overdue on the fly.
